reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Represents hypopituitarism from ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage and hypotension
The enlarged, vascularly demanding pituitary of pregnancy is especially vulnerable to hypoperfusion, explaining the peripartum timing
An early clue is failure of lactation after delivery due to prolactin deficiency, often followed by failure to resume menstruation
Presentation may be acute in the peripartum period or, more commonly, insidious over months to years with fatigue, cold intolerance, and features of combined hormone deficiency
Multiple anterior pituitary axes are usually affected, producing secondary hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency, and hypogonadism
Secondary adrenal insufficiency is the most dangerous deficit and can precipitate life-threatening crisis, particularly during intercurrent illness or stress
Diagnosis combines a suggestive obstetric history with low target hormones alongside inappropriately low pituitary trophic hormones and supportive pituitary imaging
When replacing hormones, glucocorticoid must be started before or with thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis
reference.pathophysiology: Sheehan syndrome arises when massive obstetric haemorrhage and circulatory collapse cause ischaemic infarction of the anterior pituitary. During pregnancy the gland hypertrophies, largely through lactotroph expansion, increasing its metabolic demand while its portal blood supply remains vulnerable; a sudden fall in perfusion pressure can therefore produce necrosis. Loss of anterior pituitary tissue results in deficiency of multiple trophic hormones, so the thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal axes fail secondarily, and prolactin deficiency impairs lactation. The posterior pituitary is usually spared, though partial diabetes insipidus is occasionally described. Over time the necrotic gland may involute, sometimes producing an empty sella.
additionalDifferentials: Pituitary apoplexy from a pre-existing adenoma
Other causes of hypopituitarism (tumour, infiltration, prior surgery or radiotherapy)
Primary hypothyroidism and primary adrenal insufficiency
Postpartum depression or chronic fatigue for the nonspecific presentation
additionalInvestigations: Anterior pituitary hormone panel: TSH and free T4, morning cortisol and ACTH, gonadotropins and oestradiol, prolactin, IGF-1
Dynamic testing of the adrenal axis where baseline results are equivocal
Serum electrolytes and glucose (hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia may be present)
Pituitary MRI, which may show a small or empty sella
Assessment of posterior pituitary function if polyuria is present
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, and collapse requiring emergency glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation
Acute peripartum presentation with haemodynamic instability
Starting thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid replacement, which can precipitate adrenal crisis
reference.prognosis: With timely recognition and lifelong hormone replacement, patients can live well, but the condition is often diagnosed late; unrecognised secondary adrenal insufficiency carries a real risk of fatal crisis during stress or illness.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis for years because symptoms are nonspecific and the obstetric event may be remote
Overlooking failure of lactation as an early diagnostic clue
Replacing thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid and precipitating crisis
Failing to increase glucocorticoid cover during intercurrent illness, surgery, or stress
Attributing hyponatraemia to other causes without considering hypopituitarism
